metaDescription: Six RV water heaters that run on 12V DC compared: tank DSI units, propane tankless and a dual-power 10 liter, with battery draw and fit advice.
expertTake: The Suburban SW12DEL is the best choice if you want a proven tank heater that uses 12V only to light and switch, and it keeps working on propane with no inverter. The Fogatti InstaShower 8 Plus is the pick for owners ready to go tankless and gain cabinet space. Anyone planning to heat water straight from a battery bank should skip the idea, because heating with 12V electricity is wildly inefficient.
introParagraphs: The phrase 12V RV water heater confuses many buyers. In nearly every case the 12 volts do not heat the water. They power the spark module, the gas valve, a fan or a remote switch, while propane does the actual work.

That distinction decides which heaters are sensible. A unit that burns propane and sips battery current is practical, while a heater that tries to boil water on 12 volts demands cables and amps most RVs do not have.

products.name: Suburban SW12DEL 12-gallon DSI heater with 12V relay
products.description:
The SW12DEL is a conventional tank heater whose 12V circuit does two small jobs: it powers the spark ignition and operates a relay so you can switch the heater from inside the rig. The heating itself comes from a propane burner or a 120V element, which is exactly how an RV should heat water. Twelve volts is the key that lights it, not the fuel.

Because the battery load is tiny, the SW12DEL is friendly to modest battery banks. The weak spot is voltage sag: when a house battery drops toward 10.5V the module may fail to light, which feels like a dead heater. Compared with the Fogatti and ORBEK tankless units in this guide, it stores 12 gallons ready to use and has no demand-flow requirement, but it takes up more cabinet space and weighs about 100 pounds when full of water.

Ownership includes a yearly anode rod check, a tank flush and burner tube cleaning. The relay is a separate part, so if the inside switch does nothing, test the 12V feed before blaming the heater. For most rigs with an existing 12 gallon cutout, this is the lowest-risk way to stay on propane with a tiny electrical footprint. If you tow often, drain the tank before leaving camp to shed that weight.
products.bestFor: Rigs with a 12 gallon cutout and an inside heater switch.
pros: 12V use limited to ignition and relay
Stored hot water without flow limits

products.name: Fogatti InstaShower 8 Plus propane tankless, 12V DC
products.description:
Fogatti's InstaShower 8 Plus is a propane tankless heater that runs its controls and ignition on 12V DC and is marketed as able to replace any RV water heater with a choice of door sizes. A tankless design heats water as it flows, so there is no tank to drain, no anode rod to pull and a lot of freed-up cabinet volume. For a long shower day, you are no longer limited to ten or twelve gallons.

The tradeoffs are flow and pressure. Tankless heaters need a minimum flow to fire, and a weak RV pump or a clogged aerator can leave you with a heater that cuts out mid-rinse. High-altitude readiness is a plus for mountain travel, since combustion changes with thin air. Compared with the cheaper Fogatti 7, the 8 Plus is the more capable variant in the lineup, and against the ORBEK it trades raw 60,000 BTU capacity for a simpler path.

Ownership differs from a tank. Instead of anode rods, you descale the heat exchanger, keep the vent clear of nests and watch the 12V supply, since the fan and electronics need steady voltage. Winterizing is easier because there is no large tank to drain, but you must blow out the lines. Many owners pair a tankless unit with a small accumulator or water filter to smooth flow.
products.bestFor: Owners who want unlimited hot water and more cabinet space.
pros: Heats on demand without tank limits
12V DC runs controls and fan only
cons: Needs minimum flow to stay lit

products.name: ORBEK 60,000 BTU propane tankless heater, 12V DC
products.description:
The ORBEK is built around a 60,000 BTU propane burner, which is the largest burner in this guide. Higher output means a higher flow rate at the same temperature rise, so it can support a shower and a sink at once more readily than a lower-output unit. Optional door panels, sold separately, help it fit different RV cutouts.

That output is also the concern. A 60,000 BTU burner draws a lot of propane when it is running, and your regulator, line size and tank must keep up. It also needs good venting and a flame arrestor-friendly environment. Compared with the Fogatti InstaShower 8 Plus, it offers more capacity but less track record in the RV owner community. Priced in the lower middle tier, it is a value move for people who want maximum output.

Ownership requires the same discipline as any tankless: clear the vent, descale regularly, and treat low pressure as a fault to fix rather than live with. Confirm that your propane supply can feed the burner before you buy. Check that your gas hose and regulator are rated for the higher flow before you buy.
products.bestFor: Large families or long showers where flow rate matters.
cons: Heavy propane draw at full output
Newer to the market than Suburban

products.name: VEVOR 42,000 BTU RV propane tankless heater
products.description:
VEVOR's tankless heater uses segmented combustion, which stages burner sections up and down to hold temperature as flow changes. It outputs 42,000 BTU, comes with a 15 by 15 inch door and adds an LED touch display for setting temperature. That control panel is a real step above a basic dial.

It sits between the high-output ORBEK and the more modest tank heaters. A 42,000 BTU burner is plenty for one shower plus a tap but may strain with two showers. The price tier is the lowest among the tankless units here, which is the argument for it. The caution is track record, since a newer brand means you lean on the seller for support.

Ownership is standard tankless care: descale, keep the vent open, supply stable 12V and enough propane pressure. If the heater cycles on and off, check flow rate before assuming a defect. Setting the display temperature slightly below the maximum also reduces scale buildup over time.
products.bestFor: Budget-minded tankless buyers who want a digital readout.
pros: Lowest tier of the tankless picks

products.name: Fogatti InstaShower 7 propane tankless heater
products.description:
The InstaShower 7 is the earlier, simpler Fogatti. It is pitched as a drop-in replacement without cutting into the rig, with a choice of door sizes, and it delivers hot water on demand. For owners who want tankless without paying for the Plus features, it fills the middle ground.

Against the 8 Plus, it lacks the more advanced capability the newer model advertises, so check altitude and flow specs against your travel plans. It is priced a little above the VEVOR but below the premium picks in the group. Like the other tankless units, it needs minimum flow to fire and clean venting.

Ownership is routine tankless care: descale on schedule, keep nests out of the vent, and verify 12V supply. If your rig lives near sea level and you are retrofitting, it is a sensible entry. Photograph the original cutout and measure twice, since the door size options are what make or break a clean install.
products.bestFor: Sea-level campers wanting a simple tankless swap.

products.name: Dual-power 10-liter 12V 200W / 120V 1500W heater
products.description:
This compact tank is the one product here that actually tries to heat water from 12V, at 200W, with a 1500W mode on 120V AC. Ten liters is about 2.6 gallons, which suits sink use or a quick rinse rather than a full shower. The dual-power design is aimed at caravan camping.

The physics are unforgiving. A 200W element at 12V draws roughly 17 amps, and heating a few gallons by even 50 degrees takes a long time, so battery drain is steep. It makes sense only for small tasks or when you are driving with the alternator running. The price tier is mid-range for a heater of this size.

Ownership is simple but demands care: protect it from freezing, flush periodically and watch battery state. Treat it as a niche accessory, not a whole-rig solution. It works best as a secondary heater at a camp sink beside a main propane unit.
products.bestFor: Small sink tasks and van or caravan builds.

buyingCriteria.explanation: In the Suburban SW12DEL, Fogatti and ORBEK, 12 volts powers ignition, fans and controls while propane heats the water. Only the dual-power 10 liter tank tries to heat on 12V at 200W, about 17 amps. Know which design you are buying. A quick sanity check: 200 watts at 12 volts is about 17 amps, so a ten minute rinse costs nearly 3 amp-hours from a battery that may only have 100 usable.

Spark modules and fans need steady voltage, and many fail to light below roughly 10.5V. A tired battery or a loose terminal is the top cause of ignition faults. Check your battery and cables before blaming the heater. Wire gauge matters too, because thin or long runs drop voltage under the surge of a fan starting, and the heater reads that dip as a fault.

The Suburban SW12DEL stores 12 gallons, while the tankless units heat as water flows. Tankless frees cabinet volume but needs minimum flow and steady pressure. Tanks are forgiving of weak pumps. A practical test is to run the shower at a normal flow and see whether your current fixtures deliver the flow tankless units want; if the faucet barely trickles, stay with a tank.

The ORBEK at 60,000 BTU and the VEVOR at 42,000 BTU differ by about 40 percent in heating capacity. A higher BTU allows more simultaneous use but burns more propane. Match output to how many taps you run at once. Propane lines and regulators also limit tankless output, so a 60,000 BTU burner on an undersized regulator behaves like a smaller one.

The Fogatti 8 Plus and ORBEK advertise high-altitude readiness. Thin air changes combustion and can cause poor performance in units not designed for it. Keep vents free of nests. Roughly speaking, air thins about 3 percent per 1,000 feet, so a camp at 8,000 feet changes combustion enough to trip some heaters.

Tankless units ship with door options such as the VEVOR's 15 by 15 inch panel and Fogatti's three sizes. The tank heater uses a flush-mount door. Measure your cutout before ordering. Gas and vent clearances are set by the manufacturer, so match the dimensions to the instructions rather than the old unit by eye.

howWeEvaluated.title: 12V role
howWeEvaluated.description: We checked what the 12V circuit does in each design. Most use it for controls, while one tank uses it as a heat source.

howWeEvaluated.title: Heat output
howWeEvaluated.description: We compared burner ratings, from 42,000 BTU in the VEVOR to 60,000 in the ORBEK, plus stored volume in the tank.

howWeEvaluated.title: Fit and retrofit
howWeEvaluated.description: We looked at door options and drop-in claims for each unit. Retrofits that avoid cutting into the sidewall received the most credit.

howWeEvaluated.title: Maintenance profile
howWeEvaluated.description: Anode rods, descaling and vent care were weighed per type. A tank unit asks for one anode check a year, while a tankless asks for a descale and vent check, and we scored the effort honestly.

howWeEvaluated.title: Value across tiers
howWeEvaluated.description: We judged what each price tier buys, from the VEVOR to the Suburban.

cards.label: Tank
cards.text: The Suburban SW12DEL stores 12 gallons and tolerates weak pumps, but uses cabinet space and needs anode care.

cards.label: Tankless
cards.text: The Fogatti, ORBEK and VEVOR give endless hot water and free space, but need flow and descaling.

howToChoose.note: Weak pump, choose the tank; strong pressure, choose tankless.

cards.label: Look for
cards.text: Low battery draw and propane operation, so power loss never means cold water.

cards.label: In this comparison
cards.text: The Suburban SW12DEL and the tankless units all run on propane with small 12V loads. Avoid the dual-power 10 L for real showers.

cards.label: Spend more if
cards.text: You want proven reliability, pointing to the Suburban SW12DEL, or high capacity, pointing to the ORBEK.

cards.label: Save if
cards.text: You can accept a newer brand, pointing to the VEVOR.

maintenance.why: Scale lowers flow and efficiency. Descaling extends tankless life.
Applies to the Suburban. Sediment lowers recovery.
Only the Suburban uses one. Replace at about 75 percent consumed.
Nests cause poor combustion. Keep air paths clear.
Low voltage stops ignition. Keep terminals clean.

faq.a: Only the small dual-power tank does, at 200W. That is about 17 amps, so use it for small tasks. It is useful only when driving, with the alternator or a DC-DC charger supplying the current.

faq.q: Do tankless heaters work with a weak pump?
faq.a: Often not. They need minimum flow to fire. A stronger pump or a clean aerator may help. Cleaning the faucet aerator and checking the pump pressure switch are the two cheapest fixes to try first.
Tiers run from the VEVOR at the low tankless end to the Suburban at the top. Prices change, so check listings.
A tank drains easily, but tankless units need lines blown out. Never leave antifreeze in the heater. Blowing out lines with low-pressure air is the safest tankless winter routine.
No. It lets you run more taps but burns more propane. Match it to use. A bigger burner can also cycle more often at low flow, which some owners find noisy.
No. Tanks are simple, forgiving and easy to service.
